Lesson 1 of 35 · Module 0, The Second Game: The Second Game Is the Only Score

Most people who teach board games keep score on the wrong thing. They ask themselves whether they covered every rule, whether anyone got a rule wrong, whether the game was played properly.

The one idea: A teach is not judged by how much the newcomer understood. It is judged by one thing: whether they say yes to the next game.

Read lesson 1 →

Your drill: Think back to the last three times you taught a game to someone new. For each one, write down a single word: did they ask to play again, agree when you asked, or find a reason not to?

Lesson 2 of 35 · Module 0, The Second Game: The Newcomer's Ledger

Gamers think of a teach as free. You give your time, they give their attention, and then the fun starts.

The one idea: A newcomer keeps a ledger while you teach. Every confusing minute, strange word, and public correction goes in the cost column, and the fun has to clear the total before they will play again.

Read lesson 2 →

Your drill: Write down the three things your most reluctant friend dislikes about learning games. If you do not know, ask them this week, and just listen.

Lesson 3 of 35 · Module 0, The Second Game: You Are the Host, Not the Referee

You know your favorite game cold. That is exactly the problem.

The one idea: Once you know a game, you cannot remember not knowing it. So you over-explain the rules and under-explain the point. Your job is not to guard the rules. It is to hand over confidence.

Read lesson 3 →

Your drill: Record yourself explaining a game you love in one minute, on your phone, to an imaginary friend who has never played. Play it back and count the hobby words and the rules nobody needed yet.

Lesson 4 of 35 · Module 1, Pick: Match the Game to the Person

Search for "board games for beginners" and you get the same list everywhere. The lists are not wrong.

The one idea: Do not pick a game for a newcomer. Pick a game for this newcomer: start from what they already enjoy, then fit it to tonight's time and tonight's headcount.

Read lesson 4 →

Your drill: Choose one person you want to play with more. Answer the three questions for them, then write a shortlist of three games: a sure thing, a stretch, and a wild card.

Lesson 5 of 35 · Module 1, Pick: The Teachability Scorecard

Ask a gamer which games are good for beginners and you will usually get the light ones: short rules, small box, simple components. That is a fair first guess, and it misses a lot.

The one idea: How light a game is and how teachable it is are different questions. Score a game on seven yes-or-no questions about the newcomer's experience, and the ones it fails tell you what your teach has to fix.

Read lesson 5 →

Your drill: Score five games you own on the Teachability Scorecard, at the player count you usually have. Rank them, and circle the top one: that is your next game for a newcomer.

Lesson 6 of 35 · Module 1, Pick: Build a Ladder, Not a List

Most hosts think one game ahead. They pick tonight's game, teach it, and hope.

The one idea: Plan the next four games for one person, not just tonight's. Each rung adds exactly one new idea to what they already know, so every new game feels half familiar.

Read lesson 6 →

Your drill: Write a four-rung ladder for a partner or a parent. For each rung, name the one new idea it adds in a few plain words.

Lesson 7 of 35 · Module 1, Pick: Read the Room on the Night

You picked the perfect game on Tuesday. On Saturday, your sister brings her kids, two friends arrive an hour late, and everyone is on their second glass of wine by the time the box is open.

The one idea: The game you planned is a guess made days ago. Walk in with three plans, and let the room on the night choose between them.

Read lesson 7 →

Your drill: Write plan A, plan B, and plan C for your next gathering, and the one sign that would move you from each plan to the next.

Lesson 8 of 35 · Module 2, Prep: The Solo Run

You cannot teach a game from the rulebook. You can only teach it from your head.

The one idea: The places you stumble while learning a game alone are the places your newcomer will stumble. Write them down before you forget them, and build your teach around them.

Read lesson 8 →

Your drill: Pick the next game you plan to teach. Do a solo run: read the rules once, set up for two, play three turns from both seats, and write down your three stumbles within the hour.

Lesson 9 of 35 · Module 2, Prep: Write the Five-Minute Teach Script

Most people teach a game the way they would give directions to a friend's house: from memory, out loud, adding details as they occur to them. The details pile up.

The one idea: A teach you have only thought about will run long. A teach you have written in six fields and read aloud against a timer will fit, because you cut it before anyone is waiting.

Read lesson 9 →

Your drill: Write a teach script for one game you want to teach soon. Read it aloud with a timer running, then cut until the theme, the win, the turn and the gotcha fit inside five minutes.

Lesson 10 of 35 · Module 2, Prep: Set the Table Before They Arrive

Picture the start of most game nights. Guests arrive, someone opens the box, and the teacher starts punching tokens, sorting cards and reading setup steps while everyone else watches.

The one idea: Every minute a newcomer spends watching you set up is a minute of teach they sit through with nothing to do. Finish the setup before they arrive, and the table itself starts teaching.

Read lesson 10 →

Your drill: Before your next game night, run the Pre-Flight Checklist with the game you plan to teach. Afterward, write down the one thing you forgot or the one question the setup answered for you.

Lesson 11 of 35 · Module 2, Prep: Translate the Jargon

Hobby gamers speak a dialect. Worker placement, deck building, tableau, engine, victory points, meeple.

The one idea: Every hobby word in your teach is a small test the newcomer did not sign up for. Say what the thing does, in words they already use, and the test disappears.

Read lesson 11 →

Your drill: Take your favorite game and list the five hobby words you would normally use to teach it. Write a plain replacement for each, then teach one turn out loud using only the replacements.

Lesson 12 of 35 · Module 3, The Five-Minute Teach: The Theme in One Sentence

The first thing you say when you teach a game sets the mood for everything after it. " Those are true.

The one idea: Your first sentence decides whether the rules that follow are a list or a story. Give your guest a role, a goal and a little fun, and every rule has somewhere to land.

Read lesson 12 →

Your drill: Write theme sentences for five games you own. Check each one for a role, a goal and a little fun. Then say one of them to someone who has never played, and watch their face.

Lesson 13 of 35 · Module 3, The Five-Minute Teach: How You Win

Picture learning a sport by having someone explain the rules for ten minutes before they tell you what counts as a goal. Every rule floats.

The one idea: Say how the game ends and who wins before you say how to play. Once your guest knows the finish line, every rule after it comes with a reason attached.

Read lesson 13 →

Your drill: Write a win sentence for the same five games you wrote theme sentences for: the game ends when X, the winner has the most Y. Then list each game's ways to score, biggest first.

Lesson 15 of 35 · Module 3, The Five-Minute Teach: The One Gotcha

Every game has one rule that bites. Not the hardest rule, and often not even an important-sounding one.

The one idea: Every game has one rule that punishes a newcomer for doing the natural thing. Name that one rule before play starts, name it again the first time it is about to matter, and leave every other exception for later.

Read lesson 15 →

Your drill: Go along your shelf and write one gotcha for every game you own, in a sentence you could say aloud. Check yours against the Gotcha Index, and for any game it does not list, run the cheated test on your answer.

" You will never get to everything, and you should not try. The rest of the rules arrive during the game, each one at the moment it matters.

The one idea: Most rules are better taught the moment they happen than before the first move. Hold them back, unless knowing the rule would change what a sensible player does before it comes up.

Read lesson 16 →

Your drill: Pick one game you teach often and list every rule you will hold back. Next to each one, write the moment you will teach it. Then run the test on each: would knowing it change a sensible first move? Move any yes back into the teach.

Lesson 17 of 35 · Module 3, The Five-Minute Teach: Delivery

You can write a perfect teach script and still lose the table. Delivery is where the script meets real people, with drinks in hand and phones nearby.

The one idea: The same words land differently at a different pace and aimed at a different person. Teach slowly, in short sentences, to the quietest newcomer at the table, and check in with questions that invite an answer.

Read lesson 17 →

Your drill: Teach a game to one friend, then hand them the Newcomer Feedback Card and ask its questions. Listen without explaining or defending. Write down the one answer that surprised you.

Lesson 18 of 35 · Module 4, Play: The Open First Round

" It ends when everyone can play without you. Between those two moments sits the first round, and that round can either be a test or a rehearsal.

The one idea: The first round is the second half of the teach. Play it in the open, with hidden things shown and thinking said aloud, so asking for help is part of the game, then offer a fresh start.

Read lesson 18 →

Your drill: Run one open first round at your next game night. Afterward, write down who asked what, in a few words each. The questions are a map of where your teach was thin.

Lesson 19 of 35 · Module 4, Play: Training Wheels

The principle First win early says one good decision in the first ten minutes makes the game feel like theirs. " If you tell the newcomer what to do, the move works, and they learn that the game is something you play through them.

The one idea: A newcomer's first good move should be theirs. Narrow the choice to two decent options, let them pick, and point out the payoff when it lands, so the credit stays with them.

Read lesson 19 →

Your drill: Pick one game you will teach soon and plan the first-ten-minutes move: the moment a newcomer is likely to face a real choice, the two decent options you will offer, and the payoff you will name when it lands.

Lesson 20 of 35 · Module 4, Play: Mistakes, Yours and Theirs

Rules mistakes happen in every first game. Someone moves a piece where it cannot go.

The one idea: When a rule goes wrong, protect the person before the rulebook. Let past mistakes ride, own your own errors in one sentence, and fix what comes next, never what already happened.

Read lesson 20 →

Your drill: Write a let-it-ride policy for one game you teach often: which mistakes you will let ride, which you must fix, and the exact sentence you will say. Keep it on the back of your teach script.

Lesson 21 of 35 · Module 4, Play: No Blowouts

There are two ways to ruin a newcomer's first game while playing it. The first is obvious: you crush them.

The one idea: Play hard enough to be fun and never hard enough to crush. A newcomer can forgive a loss they understand; they cannot forgive a loss that made them feel like a spectator.

Read lesson 21 →

Your drill: Look up the final scores of the last three games you played with a newcomer. Write down the gap between your score and theirs, and next to each one, the moment you think the game was decided.

Lesson 22 of 35 · Module 4, Play: Reading the Table Mid-Game

The fourth number this program holds you to is that the newcomer is never out of the game before it ends. That does not only mean eliminated by the rules.

The one idea: A game ended early on a good moment beats a game finished badly. Watch for the signs that someone has checked out, and have your exit planned before you need it.

Read lesson 22 →

Your drill: Before your next game night, decide your call-it signal: the one sign that tells you to end the game early, and the exact words you will say when you see it.

Module 5: Close starts today. By the end of it you will be able to leave every game night with the next one on the calendar.

Lesson 23 of 35 · Module 5, Close: The Debrief

The game ends, the scores are counted, and somebody reaches for the box. This is the most valuable minute of the night, and most hosts spend it packing up.

The one idea: After the game, ask what they liked, not whether they liked it. The answer tells you which game to bring next, and saying it out loud helps the newcomer remember the night as fun.

Read lesson 23 →

Your drill: Script three debrief questions for the next person you teach: one about a moment, one about next time, and one of your own. Write them on a card and keep it in the game box.

Most second games die in the hallway. " Everyone agrees.

Your drill: Pick one person you want to play with more. Write your close for them in three lines: the game, the day, and the one sentence that ties it to something they enjoyed tonight.

Lesson 25 of 35 · Module 5, Close: Keep the Streak

One great game night is a good evening. A second one is a pattern.

The one idea: A habit runs on a fixed day and familiar people, with one new thing at a time. And a newcomer becomes a player for good the day they teach a game to someone else.

Read lesson 25 →

Your drill: Put the next three game night dates on a calendar today, and send them to the people you want there. Pick the same day of the week for all three.

Module 6: The Field Guide starts today. By the end of it you will be able to teach kids, cooperative games, party games, heavy games, mixed tables, and games you have never played.

Lesson 26 of 35 · Module 6, The Field Guide: A Full Table of Newcomers

Most of this program pictures one newcomer at a table of people who know the game. This lesson is for the other night: you open the box, and every face around the table is new to it.

The one idea: When nobody else knows the game, you cannot be teacher and player and referee at once. Play slowly, recruit the fastest learner as your second teacher, and start with a game where people learn on teams.

Read lesson 26 →

Your drill: Plan a newcomers-only night: pick the game, decide who you will seat beside whom, and write down the one line you will use to ask your fastest learner for help.

Lesson 27 of 35 · Module 6, The Field Guide: Mixed Tables

A mixed table looks like the easy case. You have a newcomer, but you also have two or three people who already know the game.

The one idea: At a mixed table, the risk is not the newcomer. It is the gamers, who mean well and talk over the teach. One voice teaches, strategy waits until the game ends, and seating turns gamers into helpers.

Read lesson 27 →

Your drill: Before your next mixed game night, send your experienced players a short message with three asks: let one person teach, keep strategy until the end, and help the person beside you without playing for them.

Lesson 28 of 35 · Module 6, The Field Guide: Teaching Kids

Teaching a child a board game is the same job as teaching any newcomer, with one big difference: kids do not pretend. An adult who is lost will nod and smile.

The one idea: Kids are the most honest newcomers there are. They show you the moment a teach loses them. Match the game and the teach to the child in front of you, using age only as a starting guess.

Read lesson 28 →

Your drill: For each child you play with, pick one game that fits them now, using the age on the box as a floor, not a target. Then write down one rule you will leave out or simplify for the first play.

Lesson 29 of 35 · Module 6, The Field Guide: Cooperative Games Without a Quarterback

Cooperative games look like the perfect first game for a newcomer. Nobody can crush them, the whole table cheers together, and a loss belongs to everyone.

The one idea: In a cooperative game the active player makes the call, and everyone else may only ask questions. The teacher holds the rules, not the plan.

Read lesson 29 →

Your drill: Run one cooperative game with the one-voice rule: the active player speaks first and decides, and everyone else, you included, may only ask questions until they do.

Lesson 30 of 35 · Module 6, The Field Guide: Party and Word Games: Teach by Playing

Party and word games are the friendliest games you own, and they are the easiest to over-teach. The rules fit on a card.

The one idea: Party games are learned by watching a round, not by hearing the rules. Give sixty seconds of rules, play one demo that does not count, and let the first real round finish the teach.

Read lesson 30 →

Your drill: Teach a party game in under a minute of talking. Time it. Then run one demo round that does not count, and start the real game.

Lesson 31 of 35 · Module 6, The Field Guide: Heavier Games: Teach in Two Sittings

The program's teach takes under five minutes. Some games will not fit, and you should not force them.

The one idea: A game too big for a five-minute teach gets two short teaches instead of one long one. Teach the core, play four turns, stop and restart, then teach the rest.

Read lesson 31 →

Your drill: Pick one heavy game you own and write its core rule set: only the rules a player needs for their first four turns. Then list everything that waits for the second sitting.

Lesson 32 of 35 · Module 6, The Field Guide: When You Do Not Know It Either

Every lesson so far has assumed you know the game. Some nights you do not.

The one idea: When nobody knows the game, do not read the rulebook aloud to the table. One person reads a section ahead, the table watches one short video, and round one is played from the summary.

Read lesson 32 →

Your drill: The next time a new game comes out of the shrink wrap, try the learn-together steps once: one reader, one short video, round one from the summary, and a restart offered after it.

Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

Module 7: The Capstone starts today. By the end of it you will be able to teach one non-gamer, score your own teach, and earn the title Expert Game Guide.

Lesson 33 of 35 · Module 7, The Capstone: The Teach Library: Teach From a Sheet

Nearly every game course in the Ludarium Academy comes with a one-page teach sheet. They live together in the Teach Library, ready to print.

The one idea: A teach sheet is a reference, not a script. Read it before the night, teach from your mouth, and use the page to point at. Then edit it until it sounds like you.

Read lesson 33 →

Your drill: Pick a game from the Teach Library, teach it once from its sheet, then mark up the printout: one line you never said, one line you wish you had, and the gotcha you would move to the top.

Levi

The Ludarium

Busy stretch? Pause your Academy lessons for two weeks. They pick up where you left off.

Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

Lesson 34 of 35 · Module 7, The Capstone: Score Your Own Teach on Ten Lines

You cannot watch yourself teach. You are too busy doing it, and the curse of knowledge makes your own explanations sound clearer to you than they are to anyone else.

The one idea: Score your teach on ten lines, one to five each, within an hour of the game ending. The total matters less than the lowest line: that is the one to work on next time.

Read lesson 34 →

Your drill: Print the Self-Assessment before your next teach. Within an hour of the game ending, score all ten lines, circle the lowest, and write one sentence on what you will do differently there.

emails.html:
Hi {{ subscriber.first_name | default: "there" }},

Lesson 35 of 35 · Module 7, The Capstone: The Capstone: Earn the Title

You have learned to pick a game, prep it, teach it in five minutes, run the first game, and close with the next one on the calendar. Now you do all of it once, for one person, and tell the Guild how it went.

The one idea: To earn the title, teach one person who does not play games, and report back with the plain truth. The title is earned when they say yes to a second game.

Read lesson 35 →

Your drill: Choose your newcomer and your game this week, put the date on the calendar, and print the Self-Assessment and the Feedback Card. After the game, submit the capstone.

Levi

The Ludarium

P.S. This is the last lesson. Your final step is the capstone: teach one newcomer and tell us how it went. If they said yes to another game, you earn the title Expert Game Guide.

Busy stretch? Pause your Academy lessons for two weeks. They pick up where you left off.
